opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core challenge with physical AI is data. For language models, we had the whole internet, trillions of tokens of text that people had already written. For robots, autonomous vehicles, and other embodied systems, there's no equivalent. Collecting real-world interaction data is slow, expensive, and sometimes dangerous. You can't crash a thousand cars to learn what a near-miss looks like.

So the way we think about Cosmos is as a world foundation model, a model that has learned, from a very large amount of video, how the physical world tends to evolve. Objects fall, liquids pour, people move in certain ways, light changes as the camera moves. Once you have a model that captures those regularities, you can use it in a few ways that help generalization.

First, as a data engine. You can take a small amount of real data and generate many variations: different weather, lighting, environments, object arrangements, edge cases. That diversity is exactly what helps a policy or perception model generalize instead of overfitting to the few scenes it saw.

Second, as a simulator or a kind of imagination. A robot can ask, "If I take this action, what happens next?" and the world model predicts the future. That lets you evaluate policies or do planning without always going to the real world.

Third, as a starting point. Just like people fine-tune a language model for a specific task, developers can post-train Cosmos on their own robot or their own camera setup. The general physical knowledge transfers, and you only need a relatively small amount of domain data to specialize it.

I should be honest that we're still early. Today's world models are good at visual plausibility, but physical accuracy, things like precise contact, forces, and long-horizon consistency, is still an open problem. That's a big part of why we released Cosmos openly. We think physical AI is too large a problem for any single team, and we want researchers and companies to build on it, find where it breaks, and push it forward together.

r001.rationale: It says Cosmos can generate variations and edge cases from limited real data, covering situations beyond those collected.

r002.rationale: It describes Cosmos as a starting point whose general physical knowledge transfers when developers post-train a policy for their robot or camera setup.

r003.rationale: It mentions using predictions for policy evaluation and planning, but does not say that many realistic simulated environments run in parallel to accelerate learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. The way I think about it is this: large language models got good at generalizing because they were trained on basically the entire written record of human knowledge. Robots and autonomous vehicles don't have anything like that. Every lab collects its own data, on its own hardware, in its own environment, and most of it never gets shared. So each system learns a narrow slice of the world and breaks the moment conditions change.

Cosmos is our attempt to give physical AI its own version of that foundation. We trained world foundation models on an enormous amount of video, so the model learns the regularities of the physical world. Objects persist. Things fall when you let go. Light changes as a car moves under a bridge. Once a model has internalized that, it can imagine what happens next given an action, and that becomes a general-purpose simulator you can build on.

That helps generalization in a few concrete ways. First, data. If you have a hundred demonstrations in one kitchen, Cosmos can regenerate them in a thousand kitchens, with different lighting, different clutter, different weather for a driving scene, while keeping the physics and the actions consistent. The robot sees far more variation than anyone could collect by hand. Second, evaluation. You can test a policy against rare or dangerous situations in the world model before you ever put it on real hardware. Third, planning. If the model can predict the consequences of actions, the robot can reason about which action to take, rather than just reacting.

And we made it open, because I genuinely believe no single company can cover the whole physical world. If every robotics team starts from a shared world model and post-trains it for their domain, the way people fine-tune language models today, the whole field moves faster. That is the real goal: not one model that does everything, but a common foundation so that what one robot learns about the world is not lost to the next one.

r001.rationale: The response says Cosmos can regenerate demonstrations across many kitchens and driving conditions, creating variation beyond what was collected by hand.

r002.rationale: It says robotics teams can start from and post-train a shared world model, but does not clearly state that the model’s learned representation is a starting point for training a physical-world policy model.

r003.rationale: It describes generating varied data and testing policies in a world model, but does not say that interacting with many simulated environments in parallel accelerates learning.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that an AI system operating in the physical world has to handle situations it hasn’t encountered before. It needs some understanding of how the world evolves—how objects move, how they interact, and what might happen when it takes an action.

Cosmos can help by providing world models that generate plausible outcomes conditioned on observations or actions. That gives us a way to create more varied training experiences and test systems under different conditions. For example, a robot might practice a task with different object arrangements or lighting, rather than learning only from a small set of recorded demonstrations.

But generating more data doesn’t automatically give you generalization. The experiences need to be physically meaningful, and you still have to validate what the system learns in the real world. I see world models as a way to broaden that experience and make the process of learning and testing more scalable.

r001.rationale: It says Cosmos can generate varied training experiences, including unseen object arrangements or lighting beyond a small set of recorded demonstrations.

r002.rationale: It describes world models generating plausible outcomes, but does not say their learned representation serves as a starting point for training a physical-world policy model.

r003.rationale: It mentions making learning and testing more scalable, but does not describe interacting with many realistic simulated environments in parallel to accelerate learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the biggest challenges for physical AI is the diversity of the real world. A robot may learn to perform a task in one environment, but if you change the lighting, the objects, or the layout, it can struggle. Collecting real-world data for all those variations is very expensive.

With Cosmos, the idea is to learn a world model from video—how things move and interact—and use that model to help generate diverse training scenarios. Instead of training only on situations a robot has already encountered, we can expose it to many plausible variations, including situations that are difficult to collect in the real world.

Of course, generating realistic-looking video alone is not enough. The scenarios need to be physically meaningful, and we still need to validate the resulting behavior in the real world. But that combination of real experience, simulation, and learned world models offers a promising path toward systems that can adapt to unfamiliar situations.

r001.rationale: It says Cosmos can generate diverse training scenarios, including plausible variations that are difficult to collect in the real world.

r002.rationale: It describes learning a world model from video to generate scenarios, but does not say the model’s learned representation is a starting point for training a physical-world policy.

r003.rationale: It mentions simulation as part of a promising approach, but does not describe interacting with many simulated environments in parallel or say that this accelerates learning.
